blocks.text: The female reproductive system consists of the gonads (ovaries), oviducts, uterus and vagina; the oviducts, uterus and vagina are its accessory organs.

items: Ovaries: two oval ovaries, 3 to 5 cm long and 2 to 3 cm wide, one on each side of the uterus, produce egg cells (ova or oocytes) and hormones. Their functional units are tiny sacs, the ovarian follicles, which nurture immature eggs. In an adult, one ripening follicle releases its egg each month (ovulation), and the ruptured follicle becomes a glandular corpus luteum.

Oviducts (Fallopian or uterine tubes): two tubes from the ovaries to the uterus. The released ovum enters an oviduct and is moved towards the uterus by cilia of the lining. Fertilization takes place in the oviduct, and the zygote begins mitotic divisions there.

Uterus: a hollow muscular organ with a fundus (the rounded top above the openings of the oviducts), a body (the main part) and a cervix (the lower narrow part opening into the vagina). Its wall has an outer thin perimetrium, a thick middle myometrium of smooth muscle and an inner spongy endometrium with a basal layer, whose stem cells regenerate it, and a functional layer that thickens and is shed in each menstrual cycle; in pregnancy it thickens further, the embryo implants and its vascular spaces join to form the placenta, which supplies the embryo and foetus with oxygen and food.
Vagina: a thin-walled tube 8 to 10 cm long from the outside to the cervix; the passage for the birth of a baby and for menstrual flow.

blocks.alt: A schematic front view of the female reproductive organs: the pear-shaped uterus with its rounded fundus at the top, body and narrow cervix, its wall shown in three layers (perimetrium, muscular myometrium and the inner endometrium); two curved oviducts with fringed ends next to the two ovaries, which contain follicles; and the vagina leading down from the cervix.
blocks.caption: Human female reproductive system (original diagram after Figure 17.4).
blocks.long_description: The ovaries produce eggs and hormones; their follicles nurture the eggs, and each month one ripe follicle releases its egg (ovulation) and becomes the corpus luteum. Cilia in the oviducts move the egg towards the uterus, and fertilization takes place in the oviduct. The uterus has a fundus, body and cervix; its wall has an outer perimetrium, a thick muscular myometrium and an inner endometrium whose functional layer thickens and is shed in each cycle and, in pregnancy, helps form the placenta. The vagina, 8 to 10 cm long, leads from the cervix to the outside.

blocks.text: Egg production begins before birth: oogonia (2n) in the follicles divide by mitosis into primary oocytes (2n), which begin meiosis I but stop in prophase I and stay there through childhood, for at least 10 to 14 years. At birth the ovaries hold some 2 million follicles, each with a primary oocyte. From puberty, one primary oocyte at a time resumes meiosis I and forms two unequal haploid cells: a large secondary oocyte (1n) and a small first polar body (1n). The secondary oocyte stops in metaphase II and is released at ovulation. If it is not fertilized it dies; if a sperm fuses with it, it quickly completes meiosis II in the oviduct, forming one large ovum (1n) and a small second polar body (1n).

blocks.alt: Left: spermatogenesis as a chain of cells: germline cell (2n), spermatogonium (2n), primary spermatocyte (2n), meiosis I to two secondary spermatocytes (1n), meiosis II to four spermatids (1n) and four sperms, with a sperm's head, acrosome, midpiece and tail shown below. Right: oogenesis: oogonium (2n), primary oocyte (2n) stopped in prophase I until puberty, meiosis I to a secondary oocyte and a first polar body, and, if a sperm enters, meiosis II to one ovum and a second polar body.
blocks.caption: Oogenesis (original diagram after Figure 17.5).
blocks.long_description: In the testis, germline cells divide by mitosis; some become spermatogonia, which form primary spermatocytes; each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II to form four spermatids, which mature into sperms with a head (nucleus and acrosome), a midpiece (mitochondria and a centriole) and a tail. In the ovary, oogonia form primary oocytes before birth, which stop in prophase I; from puberty one at a time completes meiosis I to give a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body; the secondary oocyte, stopped in metaphase II, is released at ovulation and completes meiosis II only if a sperm enters, giving one ovum and a second polar body.

blocks.prompt: Which cell is actually released from the ovary at ovulation?
blocks.explanation: The secondary oocyte, stopped in metaphase II; it becomes an ovum only if a sperm enters.

items: Ovaries (follicles, ovulation, corpus luteum), oviducts (cilia, fertilization), uterus (fundus, body, cervix; perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium), vagina.
Oogenesis: oogonium, primary oocyte (prophase I until puberty), secondary oocyte + first polar body, ovum + second polar body after fertilization.
